description: Operational artifact topology contract. Names the logical identities a run produces, so documentation and tooling refer to roles rather than to path strings. Physical paths are extracted from the CLI's own planner, not written here by hand.
isolation_note: Location and isolation are independent axes. A run may move without changing its isolation model, and a shared root changes the blast radius of destructive operations without changing any single run's internal layout.

isolation_models.isolated_run_tree: Each run owns a complete directory tree; nothing is shared between runs.
isolation_models.shared_root_namespaced: Runs share a parent root but each is namespaced by run id.
isolation_models.shared_pooled: Runs share storage without per-run namespacing.

artifacts.restart_role: provenance of what the run was told to do
artifacts.note: Input copies are rewritten when a run is continued, so this is not write-once.

destructive_operations: the C runtime clears the configured fresh-run log directory at startup
artifacts.destructive_scope: the configured log directory, constrained to the run tree unless overridden
artifacts.safety_note: Because this path is configurable AND the runtime clears it on a fresh run, pointing several runs at one unnamespaced log directory is a data-loss path. Any move toward a shared root must keep this namespaced per run.
artifacts.containment: validated by picurv, and re-derived independently by the C runtime immediately before the recursive delete; escaping values require io.directories.allow_unsafe_paths at both layers.

artifacts.note: Stream logs are recreated per stage rather than appended, and lock files are created and removed during a run.

artifacts.containment: validated by picurv (the same shared rule set as the log directory); escaping values require io.directories.allow_unsafe_paths, and a value naming the run root, an ancestor of it, or a reserved run directory is refused with or without that override. Unlike the log directory this path is not deleted, so there is no independent C guard for it: the runtime guard exists specifically to stand in front of PetscRMTree.

artifacts.restart_role: records the exact inputs the run used

artifacts.containment: inherits run.runtime_logs: validated by picurv and re-checked by the C runtime before the directory holding them is deleted.
destructive_operations: deleted with the log directory on a fresh run
artifacts.destructive_scope: the configured log directory, constrained to the run tree unless overridden

artifacts.note: Holds stage stream logs, post lock files, and generated wrappers.

artifacts.containment: NOT containment-validated. post.yml -> io.output_directory is resolved directly against the run directory by _post_output_directory_abs, with no check that the result stays inside the run tree. It is not deleted recursively, so this is a correctness and archivability gap rather than a data-loss path - but it is a real difference from the solver directories and is recorded rather than implied.
artifacts.note: Shipped recipes use both a flat 'viz' and a nested 'visualization/<recipe>' layout, so the second path segment is part of the configured value rather than a fixed 'visualization' parent with a recipe beneath it.

current_isolation_model_note: REMOVED. There is no enforced isolation model. Isolation between separate runs rests on distinct run ids rather than on a storage model; see default_layout and default_layout_note. The destructive-path defect that once sat here is closed and recorded under resolved_safety_history.
default_layout_note: This is the layout a run gets when the monitor io.directories values are left at their defaults. picurv containment-validates BOTH run-owned directories, log and output, through one shared rule set. The independent C guard covers only the log directory, because only that one is recursively deleted before a fresh run; it is not a second validation of the output directory. Post-processing output (post.yml -> io.output_directory) is configurable and is NOT containment-validated at all - see run.visualization.

resolved_safety_history.note: Defects that were found and closed. Kept because the enforcement they produced is only intelligible next to the failure that motivated it, and because a reader needs to know the guard is deliberate rather than incidental. Nothing here is an open defect.

entries.was: monitor io.directories.log is passed through to -log_dir with no containment validation, and on a fresh solve the C runtime calls PetscRMTree on that directory, recursively deleting it and its contents.
observed: picurv_cli/core.py emitted '-log_dir <value>' verbatim from monitor io.directories.log.
An absolute path outside the run tree was ACCEPTED by picurv validate and by run --dry-run (rc=0, no warning).
The dry-run planner reported <run>/logs regardless, so the configured destination was not visible in the plan.
entries.consequence: An accepted configuration can cause the solver to recursively delete an arbitrary directory, including one shared by other runs or holding unrelated data.

resolution.approach: picurv rejects io.directories.log and io.directories.output values that escape the run directory, target the run root, name a reserved directory, or overlap each other. An explicit io.directories.allow_unsafe_paths: true waives exactly one verdict - an absolute location outside the run tree that neither is nor contains it. Independently, src/setup.c classifies the configured log directory immediately before PetscRMTree and refuses the delete unless the verdict is contained, or is that single waivable verdict with -allow_unsafe_log_dir supplied.
implementation: src/setup.c::LogDirectoryIsSafeToWipe (applies the waiver to one verdict)
resolution.residual_risk: io.directories.restart is deliberately not containment-checked: it is a read path that may legitimately point at another run's checkpoints. And an authorization is exactly what it says - with allow_unsafe_paths: true and an absolute external log directory, the runtime will recursively delete that directory on every fresh solve. The guard establishes that the deletion was asked for, not that it is wise.
enforcement_points: reserved-flag rejection across case, solver, and monitor passthrough
dry-run planner (reports what a real run would refuse)
submission preflight over the staged .control file
the C runtime guard immediately before PetscRMTree, independent of the launcher
rejected_conditions: a value starting with '~', which nothing expands (never waivable)
escapes the run tree by relative traversal (never waivable)
resolves to the run root itself (never waivable)
resolves to a directory CONTAINING the run root, up to the filesystem root (never waivable)
a relative name that resolves outside the tree through a symlink (never waivable)
collides with a reserved run directory (config, scheduler, checkpoints, visualization)
log and output overlap, including against a defaulted value
directory values that cannot be written to a PETSc options line unambiguously (whitespace, quotes, comment markers)
an absolute location outside the run tree WITHOUT authorization - this is the only condition an authorization waives
resolution.shared_rule_set: Configuration validation and submission preflight both call evaluate_run_directories() over effective values with defaults applied, so the two cannot drift apart and both honour the override identically.
resolution.parser_contract: Staged control files are tokenized with shlex, matching PETSc's treatment of a double-quoted span as one token. Splitting on whitespace read '-log_dir "/tmp/VICTIM DIR"' as the value '"/tmp/VICTIM', which looks contained while PETSc would use the absolute path. Malformed quoting is a preflight error, never a skipped line.
resolution.waiver_rule: Waivability is decided on a typed verdict, never on message text. An earlier version matched the substring 'escapes' in the message, which silently downgraded a run-root finding to a warning; and the C guard returned safe as soon as it saw an absolute path with authorization, before any physical comparison.
